lesson_title: The Braai, the Match and the Hill: Energy and Change
hook_text: Burning wood pays out energy. So why doesn't every tree just burst into flame?
clip_script: Burning wood releases huge amounts of energy. Profitable chemistry. So here's the awkward question: why isn't every tree on fire right now? Why does your braai sit there, wood and oxygen touching, doing absolutely nothing until you strike a match? Because every reaction — even the most profitable one — charges an entry fee. Before the new bonds can form and pay out, the old bonds must be broken open, and that cost is charged UPFRONT. Chemists call it activation energy. Picture a hiking trail: your reactants live in one valley, the products in a lower valley next door, and between them stands a ridge. Doesn't matter how far downhill the destination is — you still have to climb the ridge first. The match? It's a loan. It lifts a few molecules over the ridge; their reaction pays out; that payout funds the neighbours' climb, and the fire finances itself all evening. One match, four hours of heat. And a catalyst? A tunnel through the ridge. Faster crossing — but the valleys never move, so the payout never changes.
visual_style: A braai at dusk that refuses to light, then a single match spark cascading into flame; morph into a side-view mountain trail with two valleys, hikers boosted over the ridge, and a dashed tunnel appearing through it.
mood: Curious and satisfying — an everyday mystery cracked with one picture.
pacing: Provocative question up front, steady build through the ridge image, warm self-sustaining-fire payoff.
